The authors developed a theory and conducted computational studies of nonlinear propagation properties of electromagnetic waves in double-domain negative/positive index metamaterials.
Energy flux and phase velocity of an electromagnetic wave can become contra-directed in negative-index metamaterials, resulting in 'backward waves'.
Phase matching for nonlinear optical processes involving backward waves requires the wave vectors to be co-directed, while one of the Poynting vectors appears contra-directed.

The authors proposed a metamaterial made of standing carbon nanotubes as a proof-of-principle example to engineer negative spatial dispersion and enable the coexistence of ordinary and backward waves.

The authors also explored the possibility of using readily available Raman crystals to mimic the nonlinear optical processes with backward waves, by replacing one of the coupled electromagnetic waves with elastic waves having negative spatial dispersion.
Numerical simulations demonstrated the possibility of unidirectional amplification and shaping of optical pulses through three-wave mixing with negative phonons in Raman crystals.

The authors proposed that metamaterials supporting coupled ordinary and backward waves could be used as frequency-doubling nonlinear optical metamirrors, data-processing chips, and nonlinear optical sensors.

The authors investigated the multi-parametric dependences of the numerical solutions to the set of coupled nonlinear wave equations, accounting for the counter-directed phase velocity and energy flow in one of the coupled waves.
Frequency conversion processes stemming from the nonlinear-optical coupling of contra-propagating short pulses were studied.
The authors found that the required pulse power for the extraordinary nonlinear optical processes with backward waves is achievable with commercially available lasers.
The authors discussed the results of their research at various international conferences and seminars.
The research was funded by the Air Force Office of Science and Research under grant FA9550-12-1-0298.

The performance period of the research effort was cut by one year due to the principal investigator moving from the University of Wisconsin-Stevens Point to the Birck Nanotechnology Center at Purdue University.
The authors proposed a concept of remotely actuated and all-optical controlled nonlinear optical sensors based on the described processes and materials.

The major outcome of the research is a considerable progress in the fundamental understanding of unparalleled electromagnetic processes and counterintuitive nonlinear optical effects originating from the exotic electromagnetic properties of negative index/negative spatially dispersive metamaterials.
